overview.body:
**Inanna** (*inanna*) is the Sumerian great goddess of love, war, and the planet Venus — the morning and evening star. Her cult fused the Sumerian sky-lady with a Semitic Venus deity, producing the most complex divine personality of the ancient Near East: sexual desire and reproductive power, the frenzy of battle, and the patronage of kings in a single figure.[^1] Her mythology spans the *Descent of Inanna*, the sacred-marriage songs of Dumuzi, and the Huluppu-tree episode.

The name is written 𒀭𒈹 in cuneiform. The Unicode restoration **Inanna** recovers the standard scholarly citation form; the plain ASCII *inanna* is the fallback the early domain-name system imposed, not an ancient spelling. Because the restoration adds only the conventional capital of a proper name, the entry is placed in Tier 2.[^2]

sources.citation: Black & Green, Gods, Demons and Symbols of Ancient Mesopotamia.
Electronic Text Corpus of Sumerian Literature, Oxford Oriental Institute, 1998.

the-name.body:
The name is attested in cuneiform as **𒀭𒈹** — the divine determinative with the reed-bundle sign read Inanna. Its etymology is transparently Sumerian: *nin* 'lady' + *an* 'heaven' + *ak* (genitive), giving 'Lady of Heaven'.[^1]

By the Old Akkadian period, Inanna had been so thoroughly identified with the Semitic goddess Ištar that the two names describe a single cult. The Akkadian form Ištar is etymologically unrelated to Inanna and probably derives from a Semitic Venus deity; the merger produced the great goddess known from the Epic of Gilgameš and the Descent narratives.

The ASCII form *inanna* survives only because the early domain-name system could not carry diacritics; it is a technological compromise, not an ancient spelling. The restoration **Inanna** recovers the scholarly citation form directly.

The letter-by-letter transformation runs:

- **i** → **I** — Same, capitalised
- **n** → **n** — Same
- **a** → **a** — Same
- **n** → **n** — Same
- **n** → **n** — Same
- **a** → **a** — Same

Because no distinctive diacritic or special letter is added, the name is Tier 2.

sources.citation: Black & Green, Gods, Demons and Symbols of Ancient Mesopotamia.
The Assyrian Dictionary of the Oriental Institute of the University of Chicago (CAD).

pronunciation.body:
The reconstructed pronunciation of the name is **/iˈnan.na/** — Sumerian Reconstruction.[^1]

Phoneme by phoneme:

- **I-** — Close front vowel [i], lightly stressed in the first syllable.
- **-nan-** — Alveolar nasal [n] flanked by open vowels [a].
- **-na** — Final open syllable with reduced stress.

For the modern speaker, the closest approximation is: 'ee-NAHN-nah' — stress the second syllable and keep the vowels bright.

Kindred and historical forms of the name:

- **Sumerian** — 𒀭𒈹 (Inanna), 'Lady of Heaven'
- **Akkadian** — Ištar, the East Semitic form
- **West Semitic** — Astarte, the Levantine Venus goddess

Inanna is Tier 2 because the ASCII form *inanna* already represents the same phonemic sequence; no stress mark, length mark, or distinctive letter is required to recover the spoken name. The capitalised restoration is the scholarly citation form.

sources.citation: Electronic Text Corpus of Sumerian Literature, Oxford Oriental Institute, 1998.

original-script.body:
The name is preserved in Cuneiform as **𒀭𒈹** — Sumero-Akkadian cuneiform, attested from the Uruk period onward, in Mesopotamia.[^1]

The scholarly transliteration is *Inanna*, giving the normalised reading /iˈnan.na/.

The rendering proceeds step by step:

- The name is written 𒀭𒈹 in cuneiform.
- The divine determinative 𒀭 marks the name as theonymic.
- The sign 𒈹 is read Inanna.
- The Unicode restoration Inanna is registrable in .com; the cuneiform form is not supported in the .com IDN table.

The appropriate label is 'Original Script and Scholarly Transliteration': the cuneiform is the attested writing, and Inanna is the standard scholarly reading.

sources.citation: Akkadisches Handwörterbuch (AHw).
Black & Green, Gods, Demons and Symbols of Ancient Mesopotamia.
Electronic Text Corpus of Sumerian Literature (ETCSL).

domains.body:
Inanna is the most **volatile** of the great Mesopotamian goddesses. She is the planet Venus, the morning and evening star; she is sexual desire and reproductive power; she is the frenzy of battle and the protector of kings. No other deity in the ancient Near East so thoroughly unites what later cultures would separate into Aphrodítē and Árēs.[^1]

### The Star

The eight-pointed star of Venus; Inanna is the brightest planet and the celestial sign of the goddess.

### Love and Fertility

The sacred marriage, the life-giving womb, the power that turns desire into offspring and fields into harvest.

### War

She rides into battle with weapons at her shoulders; kings claim her as their divine patron in war.

### Sovereignty

The goddess who bestows and withdraws kingship; her favour is the divine charter of Sumerian rulers.

sources.citation: The Assyrian Dictionary of the Oriental Institute of the University of Chicago (CAD).

symbols.body:
Her attributes compress the goddess's double nature — celestial and warlike, erotic and sovereign:[^1]

- **Eight-pointed star** — the sign of Venus, her planet; the star sign writes her name in cuneiform, and in art the star disk crowns her tiara.
- **Lion** — her animal and her mount: she stands upon lions as mistress of battle.
- **Reed bundle** — the cuneiform sign 𒈹 that writes her name, linking her to the marshes of Sumer.
- **Rosette** — the fertility emblem attached to her cult from the Uruk-period cylinder seals onward.

sources.citation: Black & Green, Gods, Demons and Symbols of Ancient Mesopotamia.

mythology.body:
Inanna's myths are stories of **extremity**: descent into death, demand for the impossible, and the transformation of gender and power. She is never merely an object of desire; she is desire in motion, war in motion, the star that crosses the boundary between heaven and the underworld.[^1]

### Inanna's Descent to the Netherworld

In the Sumerian *Descent of Inanna*, the goddess abandons heaven and earth to descend to the netherworld ruled by her sister Ereškigal. At each of the seven gates she is stripped of a garment or ornament until she stands naked before the throne of the dead. She is killed and hung on a hook. Her faithful servant Ninšubur persuades Enki to create two sexless beings who revive her with the food and water of life.[^2]

### Inanna and Dumuzi

The sacred-marriage songs celebrate the union of Inanna and Dumuzi, the shepherd-king. Their love ensures the fertility of the land and the legitimacy of the king. In the *Descent*, however, Inanna chooses Dumuzi to take her place in the underworld for half the year, so that his sister Geštinanna may take the other half. The myth explains the cycle of the seasons.[^3]

### The Huluppu Tree

In the myth of the Huluppu tree, Inanna plants a tree in her garden at Uruk, but it becomes infested with a snake, an Anzu-bird, and the dark maid Lilith. She appeals to Gilgameh, who slays the snake and drives off the bird and the maid; Inanna then fashions the trunk into a throne and bed.[^4]

syncretism.body:
Inanna absorbed the Akkadian *Ištar* so completely that the two are treated as a single deity across the ancient Near East. She was identified with the Canaanite *Astarte*, the Hurrian *Šauška*, the Egyptian *Qudshu*, and contributed features to the Iranian goddess *Anāhitā*. The Hellenistic cult of Aphrodite Ourania preserves strong Inanna/Ištar elements.[^1]

Kindred figures in the PuniCodex cross-tradition index include [[ishtar|Ištar]] (love / war / Venus), [[aphrodite|Aphrodítē]] (love / beauty / desire), and [[anat|ꜥAnat]] (war / battle).

sources.citation: Electronic Text Corpus of Sumerian Literature, Oxford Oriental Institute, 1998.

cultural-legacy.body:
Inanna's afterlife runs through her Akkadian form **Ištar** and her Levantine form **Astarte**. Her eight-pointed star persists in Near Eastern and occult symbolism, and her Descent has been read as a precursor to later underworld journeys.[^1]

A popular claim derives English **Easter** from her name. The derivation is not supported by scholarship: Bede explains the month-name Eosturmonath from a Germanic goddess Eostre, and no historical or linguistic chain connects Eostre with Inanna or Astarte.[^2]

Modern receptions — from nineteenth-century paintings to feminist re-readings of *Gilgamesh* — have made her the emblem of the love-and-war goddess, though the Sumerian sources present a far less domesticated personality than the modern archetype.

sources.citation: Black & Green, Gods, Demons and Symbols of Ancient Mesopotamia.
Bede, De temporum ratione 15.

archaeology.body: The most visible monument of her cult is the **Eanna** precinct at Uruk — 'House of Heaven', the sanctuary she shared with Anu — preserving the sequence of Inanna temples from the Uruk period onward, source of the archaic cylinder seals that first display her star, lion, and rosette.[^1] In Assyria her temples at Nineveh (Emašmaš) and Arbela ranked among the richest of the empire. At Mari on the middle Euphrates, the palace of Zimri-Lim preserved the 'Investiture' fresco, in which a goddess hands the rod and ring of rule to the king.

sources.citation: Black & Green, Gods, Demons and Symbols of Ancient Mesopotamia.
